newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Depositors lose as BCCI claim thrown out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Depositors lose as BCCI claim thrown out.

text.p: Former depositors in collapsed bank Bank of Credit and Commerce International SA were dealt a blow on Wednesday when a London court threw out a 550 million pounds ($896 million) claim against the Bank of England over its supervision of BCCI.

The case, brought by the liquidators of BCCI, Deloitte & Touche, alleged that the Bank had acted "dishonestly" by granting BCCI a banking licence and by not later revoking it before the bank collapsed.

The liquidators said they are considering an appeal against the judgment and legal sources said this was almost certain. The loser of the appeal is also thought likely to take the case to Britain's highest court, the House of Lords.
Deloitte & Touche said it was disappointed by the result while the Bank of England claimed it supported its contention that the claims were "misconceived".

The claim, an amalgamation of the claims of around 6,000 depositors of the collapsed bank, stemmed from the Bank of England's role as regulator and its duties towards depositors, banks and the public.
BCCI collapsed in 1991 with debts of more than $12 billion, of which depositors have received back just over $2.0 billion so far from the liquidation.
A spokesman for Deloitte said it had always been recognised "the merits of the case would have to be reviewed by the Court of Appeal."
The Bank said in a statement that the High Court judgment had confirmed "that there never was any factual basis to support the allegation that it had acted dishonestly or in bad faith."
The judge in the case, Mr Justice Clarke, said the liquidators "had no arguable case" that the Bank had acted dishonestly.
The liquidators have paid a 24.5 percent dividend and expect to make a further payment of not less than 10 percent before the end of this year or early in 1998.
They still have outstanding claims against two firms of auditors -- $3.5 billion pounds plus interest against Price Waterhouse and $1.6 billion plus interest against Ernst & Young.
Sources say part of the liquidator's claim was based on a report into BCCI prepared by Price Waterhouse in 1990 which, it as alleged, the Bank should have acted upon.
